paras: The Arkadelphia road-work shooting was a shooting affray in early March 1882, six miles south of Arkadelphia, Arkansas, in which two white men, Joe Ross and Bud Henry, shot three Black men, Lewis Smith, Aaron Clark and Ed Clark. Smith was killed outright and a second man was reported unable to recover, though one later roundup said all three died. The two white men escaped, and the story ran as a brief wire item from Memphis to Minnesota and Wisconsin.
According to the Arkadelphia special, the shooting "arose out of a quarrel while working on the settlement roads." The reports do not say what the quarrel was about or who began it.

Ross and Henry fired on the three Black men, killing Lewis Smith on the spot. The second man named, Aaron Clark, was shot six times and "cannot possibly recover," while Ed Clark was shot twice and was expected to survive. The Watertown Republican placed the shooting on March 6.
Every account ends with the statement that the white men escaped. No report of an arrest, inquest or trial, or of the fate of the two wounded men, appears in the coverage.

The news went out as a special from Arkadelphia relayed through St. Louis on March 7, and the Memphis Public Ledger printed it that day under the headline "Three Negroes Shot by Two White Men." The next day the Memphis Daily Appeal ran the same text as "Bloody Battle in Arkansas," and the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer carried it as well, the latter cut short. None of these papers added comment, and the wire named the shooters and victims but gave no racial motive beyond identifying the men as "negroes" and "white men."

A week later the item survived only as a sentence in weekly news columns, the South Kentuckian's "General News" and the Watertown Republican's "Tragical Tales," set among unrelated murders and accidents.

The Arkadelphia special reported one man killed and two wounded, one of them mortally, while the Watertown Republican said all three "were killed in an affray." The Watertown roundup also named the second shooter "Thad. Henry" rather than "Bud Henry"; the earlier and fuller wire text is the better evidence on both points.

reader.title: Arkadelphia road-work shooting
bases: Every report calls it a 'shooting affray' in which two named white men shot three Black men after a quarrel during road work, with no mob, band or posse (A1, A2, A5).

The core event (three Black men shot near Arkadelphia by Joe Ross and Bud Henry, who escaped) appears in the wire special (A1, A2) and in separately condensed weekly items (A5, A6), though all may derive from the one Arkadelphia special, and they disagree on the number killed.

accounts.label: Arkadelphia special (wire via St. Louis)
accounts.gist: Two white men shot three Black men six miles south of Arkadelphia after a quarrel while working on the roads; one died outright, one was dying, one might recover, and the shooters escaped.

accounts.label: Weekly roundup (Watertown Republican)
accounts.gist: All three Black men were killed in an affray at Arkadelphia on March 6, the shooting done by Joe Ross and Thad. Henry, both white.

framing.detail: The Memphis papers ran the special nearly verbatim, the Public Ledger under 'Three Negroes Shot by Two White Men' and the Appeal under 'Bloody Battle in Arkansas', with no comment.
Weekly papers in Kentucky and Wisconsin reduced it to a single sentence among unrelated crimes, as a 'shooting affray' or 'affray'.

versions.value: One killed outright, one shot six times and 'cannot possibly recover', one shot twice and 'may recover'

conflicts.note: The wire special is the earlier and fuller text; the Watertown roundup a week later may have compressed it. No follow-up on the wounded men was found.
Three papers give 'Bud'; only the Watertown roundup gives 'Thad.'.
